extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical/absurdist literature (fans of Rabelais)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and devices for producing bawdy, mock-heroic, and grotesque comic prose in the Rabelaisian tradition. Focuses on exaggeration, parody of erudition, absurd worldbuilding, cataloguing, and playful onomastics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ extreme, physically impossible exaggeration to produce comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pantagruel’s darts 'nearly resembling the huge beams that support the bridges' and that at 'a mile’s distance would open an oyster and never touch the edges'; the physeter pierced with dozens of beams, the flying swine with gem-like eyes. Use towering scale and literal overstatement to create absurdity and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-heroic / elevated diction applied to low subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a high, grandiloquent tone (classical allusion, formal history) to describe trivial, bodily, or kitchen-level matters, producing bathos and irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly treats sausages, cooks, and chitterlings with the gravity of imperial history and battle (e.g., comparisons to 'the Emperor Antonius Caracalla' or 'the learned have affirmed...'). This juxtaposition of register—classical references about Achilles, emperors—against vulgar subjects creates ridicule and comic contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive onomastics and punning names
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humorous character/place names by compounding, punning, or literalizing functions or body parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include colonels 'Maul-chitterling' and 'Cut-pudding', long lists of cooks (Sour-sauce, Crisp-pig, Greedy-gut, etc.), and place-names. Names themselves carry jokes and can foreshadow role/character, serving as an ongoing gag and associative humor device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerative catalogue and piling (list-comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate comedic momentum and overwhelm the reader by long, detailed lists and catalogues of similar items or names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long inventories of cooks and lard-names (Lard, Pinch-lard, Snatch-lard...) demonstrate how piling many related comic items intensifies absurdity and satirical tone. Use repetition, variations, and parataxis to escalate laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of learned erudition / pseudo-scholarly citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mock academic or classical authority by quoting or imitating scholarly arguments and then subverting them with absurd conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator invokes Pythagoreans, Plato’s Cratylus, historical emperors, and then absurdly applies syllable-count 'science' to bodies (odd/even syllables determine left/right deformity). Presenting mock-logic with authoritative language lampoons pedantry and pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd causal logic and nonsense syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use deliberately fallacious or nonsensical reasoning presented seriously to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deriving that 'Patroclus was to fall by the hand of Hector' from name-numbers, or dividing 'satyros' as 'sa Tyros' to interpret a dream as prophecy. Such faux-logical moves satirize rationalism and invite reader amusement at the gap between formality and nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque and bodily humor (scatological/visceral imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on vivid, often crude bodily images, grotesque transformations, and culinary/sexual innuendo for comic shock and earthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes feature larding beasts, Chitterlings, spilling mustard that 'restores the dead', body-part jokes, and references to 'prick-purse' and 'prick-madam'. Use sensory detail (sights, smells) and coarse imagery to anchor satire in the body and the kitchen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick / comic violence with incongruous weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage chaotic, violent action using absurd or domestic implements to create visual and situational comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fights where cooks charge with spits, frying-pans, and brooms, Friar John’s 'sow' war-machine, and the description of chopping sausages are examples. Replace weapons of war with household/kitchen tools to undercut martial seriousness and generate slapstick humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented mythology and internal worldbuilding for satirical purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Create fictional customs, gods, rituals, and economies (e.g., islands that live on wind) that mirror and mock real societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wild Island’s Carnival god, the Wind-eating island of Ruach, and customs like tribute of chitterlings are worldbuilding elements that satirize religion, economy, and ritual. Make the invented world coherent enough to sustain jokes and to allow satire by analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct address and conversational asides to the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the fourth wall with rhetorical questions, injunctions, or asides that guide reader belief and shape comic stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'You shake your empty noddles now... Believe it if you will' engage the reader, invite complicity or skepticism, and modulate tone between confession and brag, enhancing comic rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical/satirical allusion to institutions and politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Weave references to contemporary political, legal, or social institutions to satirize power and public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to 'the national Council of Chesil', 'King Charles VI', and burlesques of civic rituals (military reception, councils) show how attuning jokes to institutional targets turns fantastical comic scenes into social satire. Use specific allusions to anchor satire and to lampoon authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bathos via sudden anticlimax or reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humor by abruptly moving from an elevated expectation to a ludicrous or trivial outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military-magnitude preparations that end with mustard healing the fallen, or a terrifying flying hog that merely cries 'Carnival' and voids mustard. Use set-ups that prime grandeur and end them in comic deflation.
